basic_info.name: Phreesia
basic_info.description: Phreesia is a US cloud-based patient intake and patient-activation platform delivered through in-office tablets/kiosks (PhreesiaPad/PadX), patients' own mobile devices, and an AI voice agent (VoiceAI). It digitizes administrative pre-visit workflows - registration, insurance eligibility verification, consents, copay/balance payment, and logic-driven clinical questionnaires plus patient-reported outcomes (PHQ-9, GAD-7, HRAs, medical history) - and writes the captured data back into the provider's EHR/PM system. The single most load-bearing fact is its scale: Phreesia reported 4,744 average healthcare-services clients and more than 180 million patient visits in 2025 (about 1 in 6 US patient visits), proving that patient-facing kiosk/tablet intake works at national scale. Crucially, it is administrative and questionnaire-based only: it does not perform conversational clinical history-taking (HPI), does not digitize scanned physical documents, and does not emit a standards-based clinical summary document (no FHIR Composition/OPConsultRecord, no national record push).
basic_info.organization: Phreesia, Inc. (NYSE: PHR). Founded 2005 by Chaim Indig and Evan Roberts; headquarters currently listed in Wilmington, Delaware / Burlington, Massachusetts area, with US operations in Raleigh, North Carolina.

technical_features.what_it_does: Phreesia automates the administrative front of the visit: digital patient registration and demographics, real-time insurance eligibility and benefits verification, electronic consent capture, copay and balance payment collection, appointment scheduling/reminders, and logic-driven clinical questionnaires. Its 'intake' engine adapts questions per patient based on prior responses, and it can deliver and score patient-reported outcome and screening instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, developmental screenings, Patient Activation Measure) plus health risk assessments (HRAs) and medical-history questionnaires ahead of the visit. Captured data is pushed into the provider's EHR/PM system. It does not generate a physician-ready clinical history summary, does not synthesize a FHIR Composition/OPConsultRecord, and does not digitize scanned documents into structured clinical FHIR resources.
technical_features.architecture: Cloud-based multi-tenant SaaS. Access modalities: Phreesia Mobile (patient's own device via secure one-time link, no app/login), Phreesia PadX (in-office tablet/kiosk for waiting-room check-in), Phreesia Arrivals (front-desk workflow), and Phreesia VoiceAI (24/7 inbound call agent). Integrations are proprietary and built by a dedicated Phreesia interoperability team rather than exposed as a public/self-serve API; connection is via HL7v2, FHIR, CCD, CSV and proprietary extracts. AI is increasingly used in the product (adaptive 'smart intake' forms, VoiceAI call handling, PlanMatch, and the MediFind 'Chloe' provider-search chatbot).
technical_features.inputs: Patient-entered demographics, contact details, insurance/card images, signed consents, payment data, questionnaire/screener responses (PROs, HRAs, SDOH, medical history), appointment schedule data, and call audio for VoiceAI.
technical_features.outputs: Structured data written into the EHR/PM system of record via HL7v2 (ADT, SIU), FHIR (e.g. QuestionnaireResponse, DocumentReference, Patient, Coverage, Appointment), CCD, or CSV; scored screening/PRO results and analytics dashboards. It does not output a clinical summary Composition (no FHIR Bundle.type=document, no OPConsultRecord).
technical_features.standards_compliance: Phreesia is an HL7 Organizational Member and states it integrates using open standards - HL7v2, FHIR, CCD, CSV - plus X12 270/271 for eligibility and FHIR resources such as QuestionnaireResponse/DocumentReference. This conformance is described from published product capability rather than from a public, validated API specification (independent profiles note that Phreesia exposes no public developer portal, API reference, sandbox or documented webhooks). There is no evidence of conformance to the NRCeS FHIR IG for ABDM, OPConsultRecord, HL7 International Patient Summary, SNOMED CT, LOINC or ICD coding as an output contract. Standards use is US-centric (HIPAA, US EHR interoperability).
technical_features.offline_capability: [uncertain] Phreesia is a cloud SaaS platform and its intake, eligibility, scoring and EHR write-back all depend on network connectivity; patients complete most intake on internet-connected devices before or at arrival. No published offline-first mode, local store-and-forward, or encrypted on-device queue was found. Brief connectivity resilience during a live check-in is not documented publicly.
technical_features.languages_supported: Phreesia states its mobile intake and forms are delivered in 20+ languages and its platform supports multilingual patient communication; it is English-first and oriented to US patient populations. No evidence of Hindi, Devanagari, or code-mixed Hinglish support, and no Indic-language documentation.
technical_features.deployment_model: Cloud SaaS consumed via patients' own browsers/devices, an in-office tablet/kiosk (PhreesiaPad/PadX) supplied to the practice, front-desk tools, and VoiceAI telephony. Practices run it alongside their EHR/PM or as a partial replacement. No on-premises or edge inference hardware requirement is published; all logic and scoring run in Phreesia's cloud.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: Vendor-claimed operational figures rather than clinical-accuracy metrics: 97% fewer errors in consent form completion; up to 75% less staff time on manual data entry; intake data delivered to the EHR in 3 minutes or less; one large health system generated 233 additional Medicare Annual Wellness Visits and >$24,000 additional revenue in 90 days. No published precision/recall, F1, concept-recall, concordance or clinical-accuracy evaluation for history or summary generation - because the product does not generate clinical summaries.
performance_metrics.latency: Vendor states completed forms/data reach the EHR or PM system in 3 minutes or less via direct integration. Eligibility verification is described as real-time at check-in. No published per-interaction latency for the conversational/voice components.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Not publicly specified. As a cloud SaaS the heavy processing runs server-side; the client is an ordinary browser/tablet or phone. No kiosk RAM/CPU/GPU or on-device model footprint is documented.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: 4,744 average healthcare-services clients in Q2 FY2027 (up 277 year over year); more than 180 million patient visits enabled in 2025, about 1 in 6 US patient visits; Q2 FY2027 revenue $129.5M (10% YoY growth), total managed payments $1.626B in the quarter; ~$74.6M cash; public company with ~63.2M shares issued. Growth guided at mid-single-digit client growth for FY2027.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Figures are vendor- and customer-reported operational/ROI claims, not peer-reviewed clinical validation. There is no equivalent of a PDQI-9, ROUGE, concept-recall or blinded clinician concordance study for clinical history or summary quality, because the product does not perform summarization. Third-party review sites independently estimate pricing and re-report vendor numbers.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: Phreesia is the closest deployed analogue for the MediKiosk channel (patient-facing kiosk/tablet plus mobile pre-visit intake) and it strongly validates the channel at national scale: four thousand-plus organizations accept patient self-service intake, patients complete it, and the data writes back into clinical systems. That de-risks the MediKiosk premise that a patient-facing kiosk can be deployed inside real US-style OPD workflows. At the same time Phreesia defines the ceiling of the purely administrative approach and is therefore a sharp contrast case: it captures structured answers, screeners and PROs but never conducts conversational clinical history-taking (HPI/SOCRATES), never digitizes scanned paper documents, and never emits a standard-based physician summary document. It demonstrates there is a large, funded market for pre-visit intake while leaving Module C's core value - turning elicited history plus digitized documents into one physician-ready, standards-conformant summary - unaddressed.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) logic-driven, response-adaptive questionnaires so patients only answer relevant items - a proven way to raise completion and data quality; (2) genuinely multi-modal delivery (patient's own phone + in-office tablet + voice) as modalities of one platform, not separate vendors; (3) pre-visit completion to reduce front-desk load and have the chart ready before the encounter; (4) scoring and structured write-back of instruments into the record rather than free text; (5) the operational proof that self-service kiosk intake scales. Reject: (1) administrative-only scope as the product boundary - MediKiosk must own clinical history and summary generation; (2) cloud-dependent architecture and real-time eligibility assumptions that assume reliable connectivity; (3) closed, vendor-built integrations with no public API; (4) English-first/US-EHR orientation; (5) any drift toward billing/payments/network-solutions scope that would distract from the clinical summary mission.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: It does not do the clinical core of Module C: no conversational HPI, no diagnosis-supporting narrative, no document digitization, no clinical summary artifact, no national record push. It is cloud-only with no offline story, so it cannot satisfy MediKiosk's offline-first and India-residency constraints. Integration is closed and vendor-managed, with customer reports of slow and expensive interface projects. It is English/US-centric with no Indic-language or ABDM capability. Its clinical questionnaire content is form-based, not open dialogue, so it cannot follow up on ambiguous answers the way a conversational history engine must. There is also scope-creep risk visible in its own news (payments, marketing/network solutions) that MediKiosk should avoid.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: Phreesia strengthens the kiosk-intake concept but is largely orthogonal to MediKiosk's differentiation. Phreesia: US, cloud-only, administrative forms and PROs, closed EHR integration, no clinical history synthesis, no ABDM output, English-first. MediKiosk: India (Ministry of Ayush/AIIA), offline-first, India data residency, patient-elicited clinical history (voice + touch) plus digitized-document FHIR extraction, one bilingual physician-ready summary emitted against the NRCeS FHIR IG OPConsultRecord, per-field provenance, elicit-never-diagnose, physician attestation. Phreesia does not erode MediKiosk's stated differentiation; if anything it validates the market for pre-visit patient self-service while highlighting that no incumbent combines it with standards-conformant clinical summary generation.

business_info.license: Proprietary commercial SaaS; no open-source license. Public company (NYSE: PHR).
business_info.pricing: No published list price; quote-based per organization. Third-party estimates: starting around $250-$300 per month for smaller configurations, up to $800+/month; small-to-mid practices commonly $500-$2,500/month and enterprise health systems $5,000-$15,000+/month; additional transaction fees for texting, reminders and payments may apply. Phreesia ran a promotion making the full Intake platform free through December 31, 2026.
business_info.funding: Raised more than $100M privately (including a 2017 round led by Echo Health Ventures) before its initial public offering. IPO priced at $18.00/share on 17 July 2019, listing on the NYSE under PHR, raising roughly $130.8M net to the company. Since IPO it is funded by public markets and cash flow; it reported positive GAAP net income for FY2026 and reduced debt in FY2027.
business_info.commercial_status: Commercial public company. Profitable as of recent quarters, with positive operating and free cash flow for nine consecutive quarters and a reduced debt principal in Q2 FY2027.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: US patient-intake/RCM adjacent tools: Clearwave, Luma Health, IntakeQ, Tebra, and payment/intake consolidation plays; clinical ambient scribes (Abridge, Ambience, Nuance DAX) are adjacent but doctor-side rather than intake. In India the closest patient-side analogue is Eka Care (ABDM-native PHR plus records digitization), and Yolo HealthATM occupies the kiosk/vitals niche. No incumbent was found combining US-style intake kiosk with NRCeS-conformant ABDM summary emission, so MediKiosk's overlap with Phreesia is conceptual (channel) rather than head-to-head.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: Bidirectional integrations with leading US EHR/PM systems including Epic, athenahealth, eClinicalWorks, NextGen, Oracle Health/Cerner, Veradigm, Meditech, ModMed, Greenway and AdvancedMD, plus HIE, data warehouse and data lake targets, delivered over HL7v2, FHIR, CCD and CSV by a dedicated interoperability team. No ABDM gateway roles (HIP/HIU/PHR), no Health Locker, and no Indian EHR integrations were found.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: Phreesia sits in a consolidating US front-end intake and revenue-cycle market, extending into patient financing via the AccessOne acquisition (completed November 2025) and provider-audience marketing via ProviderConnect and the DeepIntent marketplace (September 2026). It is infusing AI across operations (VoiceAI, PlanMatch, Chloe/MediFind, AI-driven smart intake) and is positioning around patient activation and front-end revenue cycle rather than clinical documentation. None of this touches the ABDM/India market or offline clinical summary generation, so it provides market-viability evidence rather than competitive pressure for Module C.

history.release_date: Company founded/incorporated May 2005; core patient-intake product (PhreesiaPad tablet) shipped from the mid-2000s. Initial public offering priced 17 July 2019 (NYSE: PHR).
history.key_milestones: 2005 company founded by Chaim Indig and Evan Roberts; late 2018 acquired Vital Score Health; July 2019 IPO at $18.00/share; July 2023 acquired MediFind (provider directory); November 2025 completed the AccessOne acquisition (patient financing); fiscal 2026 first positive GAAP net income (~$2.3M), >$100M adjusted EBITDA and ~$50M free cash flow; 2026 accelerated AI adoption across products and operations.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: Within the last six months Phreesia: reported Q1 FY2027 results (May 2026) citing >180M patient visits enabled in 2025 (~1 in 6 US visits) and health-system AI momentum; was named to Becker's 2026 'Revenue Cycle Management Companies to Know' (April 2026); launched the AI chatbot 'Chloe' on its MediFind provider-search platform (July 2026); announced a March of Dimes partnership for prenatal/postpartum patient education (July 2026); reported Q2 FY2027 results (September 2026) with 4,744 average healthcare-services clients (+6% YoY), revenue of $129.5M (+10% YoY), fifth consecutive positive net-income quarter, ninth consecutive positive free-cash-flow quarter and >$23M of debt principal reduction; expanded ProviderConnect audiences into the DeepIntent marketplace (September 2026); and highlighted VoiceAI scaling (100,000 calls in its first two months at Evergreen Family Medicine, claiming $650,000 in cost savings). It also made its Intake platform free through the end of 2026.

market_positioning.target_users: US patients (as the intake end-user) and, as buyers, healthcare provider organizations - medical groups, specialty practices, FQHCs and large health systems - plus life-sciences companies and other organizations that use its patient-engagement channel.
market_positioning.market_segment: Patient intake / digital front door, patient activation and engagement, and front-end revenue cycle management (adjacent to, but not part of, clinical documentation or FHIR summary tooling).
market_positioning.positioning_statement: Phreesia describes itself as 'the trusted leader in patient activation, giving healthcare providers, life sciences companies and other organizations tools to help patients take a more active role in their care,' emphasizing that it enabled more than 180 million patient visits in 2025 - about 1 in 6 visits across the U.S. - and that it connects intake, payments and outreach to improve operational efficiency, cash flow and healthcare outcomes.
